results.name: single_example_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate on single-example sets minus yes-rate on multi-example sets (non-example targets only); observed above null means the model under-generalizes from one example (too narrow/conservative on n=1), below means it over-generalizes.
results.code:
# name: single_example_yes_gap
# description: Yes-rate on single-example sets minus yes-rate on multi-example sets (non-example targets only); observed above null means the model under-generalizes from one example (too narrow/conservative on n=1), below means it over-generalizes.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    a = (n == 1) & (~inset)
    b = (n > 1) & (~inset)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_proximity_gap
results.description: In single-example sets, yes-rate on targets within 15 of the example minus yes-rate on targets more than 40 away; the model has no numeric-distance term for n=1 (only one-sided bounds), so observed above null means people generalize from a single example by magnitude similarity the model misses, below means they ignore magnitude more than modelled.
results.code:
# name: single_example_proximity_gap
# description: In single-example sets, yes-rate on targets within 15 of the example minus yes-rate on targets more than 40 away; the model has no numeric-distance term for n=1 (only one-sided bounds), so observed above null means people generalize from a single example by magnitude similarity the model misses, below means they ignore magnitude more than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    dist = np.abs(E[:, 0] - t)
    ok = (n == 1) & (dist > 0)
    a = ok & (dist <= 15)
    b = ok & (dist > 40)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: first_example_digit_lift
results.description: Among multi-example sets without a shared final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the FIRST example's final digit (but not the last's) minus yes-rate on targets sharing no example's final digit; the model gives only the last example a lingering digit, so observed above null means a primacy digit effect the model misses.
results.code:
# name: first_example_digit_lift
# description: Among multi-example sets without a shared final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the FIRST example's final digit (but not the last's) minus yes-rate on targets sharing no example's final digit; the model gives only the last example a lingering digit, so observed above null means a primacy digit effect the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin = np.nanmin(D, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & (dmin != dmax) & (~inset)
    td = t % 10
    first = D[:, 0]
    last = D[np.arange(len(t)), n - 1]
    anyd = np.any(D == td[:, None], axis=1)
    a = ok & (td == first) & (td != last)
    b = ok & (~anyd)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: full_profile_match_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets (multi-example sets) that are inside [min,max] and satisfy every one of parity, multiple-of-3..10 and final digit that all examples share; observed below null means people cap their endorsement of best-fitting targets (a yes-ceiling/lapse the model's sigmoid lacks), above means the model is too lukewarm on perfect matches.
results.code:
# name: full_profile_match_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets (multi-example sets) that are inside [min,max] and satisfy every one of parity, multiple-of-3..10 and final digit that all examples share; observed below null means people cap their endorsement of best-fitting targets (a yes-ceiling/lapse the model's sigmoid lacks), above means the model is too lukewarm on perfect matches.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    ok = np.ones(len(t), dtype=bool)
    # parity
    P = np.mod(E, 2)
    allodd = np.sum((P == 1) & valid, axis=1) == n
    alleven = np.sum((P == 0) & valid, axis=1) == n
    tp = np.mod(t, 2)
    ok &= ~(allodd & (tp != 1)) & ~(alleven & (tp != 0))
    for m in range(3, 11):
        allm = np.sum((np.mod(E, m) == 0) & valid, axis=1) == n
        ok &= ~(allm & (np.mod(t, m) != 0))
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin = np.nanmin(D, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    samed = dmin == dmax
    ok &= ~(samed & (np.mod(t, 10) != dmin))
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    m = ok & (n >= 2) & (~inset) & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: unstructured_set_target_dispersion
results.description: For multi-example sets sharing neither parity nor final digit, the response-weighted mean over sets of the across-target SD of pair-level yes-rates (pairs with >=5 responses); observed above null means people discriminate between targets of weakly-structured sets more sharply than the model's near-flat overlap predicts, below means the model is too target-specific.
results.code:
# name: unstructured_set_target_dispersion
# description: For multi-example sets sharing neither parity nor final digit, the response-weighted mean over sets of the across-target SD of pair-level yes-rates (pairs with >=5 responses); observed above null means people discriminate between targets of weakly-structured sets more sharply than the model's near-flat overlap predicts, below means the model is too target-specific.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    P = np.mod(E, 2)
    samep = (np.sum((P == 1) & valid, axis=1) == n) | (np.sum((P == 0) & valid, axis=1) == n)
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    samed = np.nanmin(D, axis=1) == np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (~samep) & (~samed)
    sub = df.loc[m, ["number_set", "target", "rating"]]
    if len(sub) == 0:
        return 0.0
    g = sub.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
    g = g[g["size"] >= 5]
    if len(g) == 0:
        return 0.0
    s = g.groupby("number_set").agg(sd=("mean", lambda x: float(np.std(x))), k=("mean", "size"), w=("size", "sum"))
    s = s[s["k"] >= 3]
    if len(s) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.average(s["sd"], weights=s["w"]))

results.name: outside_range_distance_falloff
results.description: Multi-example sets, non-example targets outside [min,max]: yes-rate for targets within 10 of the nearest example bound minus yes-rate for targets more than 25 beyond it; the model's hard bounds give a flat out-of-range penalty, so observed above null means people's generalization falls off gradually with distance outside the range (a graded magnitude band the model lacks).
results.code:
# name: outside_range_distance_falloff
# description: Multi-example sets, non-example targets outside [min,max]: yes-rate for targets within 10 of the nearest example bound minus yes-rate for targets more than 25 beyond it; the model's hard bounds give a flat out-of-range penalty, so observed above null means people's generalization falls off gradually with distance outside the range (a graded magnitude band the model lacks).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    ok = (n >= 2) & (dist > 0)
    a = ok & (dist <= 10)
    b = ok & (dist > 25)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_violator_yes_rate
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples all share one final digit, the yes-rate on non-example targets with a different final digit AND opposite parity to the examples (clear violators); observed above null means people keep a floor of yes responses (guessing/lapse) the model drives too close to zero, below means the model is too lenient on violators.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_violator_yes_rate
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples all share one final digit, the yes-rate on non-example targets with a different final digit AND opposite parity to the examples (clear violators); observed above null means people keep a floor of yes responses (guessing/lapse) the model drives too close to zero, below means the model is too lenient on violators.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin = np.nanmin(D, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    samed = (dmin == dmax) & (n >= 2)
    m = samed & (np.mod(t, 10) != dmin) & (np.mod(t, 2) != np.mod(dmin, 2))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: majority_digit_containment_lift
results.description: In sets of 3-4 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets containing a digit that appears in at least half but not all of the examples, minus yes-rate on targets containing no digit from any example; the model only credits digits shared by ALL examples (plus the last example's final digit), so observed above null means people use partially-shared (majority) digit features the model misses.
results.code:
# name: majority_digit_containment_lift
# description: In sets of 3-4 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets containing a digit that appears in at least half but not all of the examples, minus yes-rate on targets containing no digit from any example; the model only credits digits shared by ALL examples (plus the last example's final digit), so observed above null means people use partially-shared (majority) digit features the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(valid, E, -1).astype(int)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def has(x, d):
        # x int array (may be -1 for missing); digit containment for 1..100
        ones = np.mod(x, 10); tens = np.mod(x // 10, 10)
        h = (ones == d) | ((x >= 10) & (tens == d))
        if d in (0, 1):
            h = h | (x == 100)
        return h & (x >= 1)
    maj = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    anyc = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for d in range(10):
        cnt = np.sum(has(Ei, d), axis=1)
        th = has(t, d)
        maj |= th & (cnt * 2 >= n) & (cnt < n)
        anyc |= th & (cnt >= 1)
    ok = (n >= 3) & (~inset)
    a = ok & maj
    b = ok & (~anyc)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
